1037.title: the mudras
1037.hook: a raised open palm on a temple image, and a lowered one beneath it: two hands that speak first
1037.carry: the raised palm that says do not fear
1037.howItsDone: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, the thumb and ring finger steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Today the hands turn around and face you.

A crossing guard steps into the road and lifts one hand, palm out, fingers up. The cars stop. Nobody says a word. Now stand before an image of Shiva as the dancer, ringed in flame. Among his hands, one is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up. Almost the crossing guard's hand. But it isn't saying stop. It's saying something gentler. So far the mudras have been things a practitioner does. Today, two you don't make. You receive them.
screen: `ONE RAISED PALM STOPS THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE SAME PALM ON SHIVA.` → `A MUDRA YOU RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: That raised, open palm is abhaya mudra. Abhaya means fearlessness, the absence of fear. The gesture says: do not be afraid. On some images, look for a second hand, lowered, palm open toward you, fingers pointing down, as if letting something fall into your hands. That's varada mudra, the gesture of giving, of granting what is asked. In some paintings of Lakshmi, coins pour from that lowered palm. One hand lifts the fear. The other gives. Now open the Bhagavad Gita to its sixteenth chapter. Krishna lists the qualities of a person whose nature leans toward the divine, and the list begins with one word: abhayam, fearlessness. Then purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge, giving, self-control. So when a devotee stands before that raised hand, the very quality the Gita names first is being held out to them. People read the gesture in more than one way. Some hear a promise: the god protects, there's nothing to fear here. Some hear an invitation: this is a quality meant to grow in the one who looks. The palm holds both. One more detail: the same raised palm and lowered, giving hand also appear on Buddhist and Jain images, each tradition reading them in its own way. A shared language of hands. And it turns the mudras around. They aren't only something you form in a quiet room. You stand in front of a hand, and it speaks first.
screen: `ABHAYA: THE PALM THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.` · `VARADA: THE LOWERED PALM THAT GIVES.` · `GITA 16: THE LIST OPENS WITH FEARLESSNESS.` · `A PROMISE, OR AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `THE HAND SPEAKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let the left hand rest beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers down: the giving hand. Raise the right hand to shoulder height, palm forward, fingers up and relaxed: the hand that says do not fear. Breathe slowly, and if a worry comes, let it meet the raised palm without arguing; if you pray, you can face a home shrine, and if not, just let the hands rest in their shapes.
The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives.
Your line: the raised palm that says do not fear. Tomorrow, the hands go on stage. Day one thousand thirty-seven, done.

1038.title: the mudras
1038.hook: a dancer tells a whole story with her hands, and an old dance manual says where the hand goes, the eyes follow
1038.carry: where the hand goes, the eyes follow
1038.howItsDone: In classical Indian dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, dancers learn named hand gestures (hastas) and use them with facial expression to tell stories, often of the gods, before an audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two mudras you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives. Today the hands start to move.

How do you say lotus without a word? A dancer on a temple stage cups her hand, fingers curved and spread, and there it is, a flower opening. A turn of the wrist, and two fingers become a deer's ears. The hand flattens, fingers together, thumb tucked, and now it's a flag, or a cloud, or a forest, depending on the story. The drum keeps time. Her face follows her hands. Anyone who knows the language of the hands can follow without a program.
screen: `A LOTUS, WITHOUT A WORD.` → `A FLAG, A CLOUD, A FOREST.` → `THE FACE FOLLOWS THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: In classical Indian dance, the hand gestures have their own name: hastas, hands. Dancers call them mudras too. One old manual, the Abhinaya Darpana, the mirror of gesture, is attributed to a teacher named Nandikeshvara. It lists hand shapes one by one, each with a name and its meanings. Pataka, the flag: the flat hand, fingers together, thumb bent in. Mukula, the bud. Bhramara, the bee. Hamsasya, the swan's beak. One shape can stand for many things; the story tells you which. Then comes a verse dancers quote, here in paraphrase. Where the hand goes, the eyes follow. Where the eyes go, the mind follows. Where the mind goes, the feeling follows. And where the feeling goes, rasa arises. Rasa means juice, flavor, taste: in the old theory of drama, the feeling the audience tastes when a performance works. So the chain runs from a hand to a feeling the whole room shares. Notice the direction. On a meditation cushion, you might think the mind leads and the hand obeys. The dancer's verse runs the other way: start with the hand, and the rest of you comes along. The same manual opens by bowing to Shiva, in paraphrase: whose body is the whole world, whose speech is all language, whose ornaments are the moon and stars. For the dancer, the stage is a small copy of that, and a hand moving in the light becomes a way of speaking about the world, and to the one who dances it.
screen: `HASTAS: THE DANCER'S HANDS.` · `A FLAG, A BUD, A BEE, A SWAN'S BEAK.` · `HAND, EYES, MIND, FEELING, RASA.` · `THE HAND LEADS, THE REST FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `WHERE THE HAND GOES, THE EYES FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Make pataka, the flag: right hand flat, fingers together, thumb bent in, held in front of your chest. Move it very slowly out to the right and back, then to the left and back, eyes following the hand, slower than feels natural. Notice whether the mind follows the eyes, the way the verse says, and when it wanders, return to the hand.
The mudras. In dance, hastas: hand shapes that tell a story, where the hand leads and the eyes, the mind and the feeling follow.
Your line: where the hand goes, the eyes follow. One more day of hands tomorrow. See you then.

1039.title: the mudras
1039.hook: a potter's hands, a cook's, a shopkeeper's: no sacred shape among them, and the Gita puts hands everywhere
1039.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1039.howItsDone: Hindus hold shaped hands in worship, practice and dance; some also reflect on Bhagavad Gita 13 and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, which describe the one reality as having hands and feet everywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday the mudras went on stage: where the hand goes, the eyes follow. Today, the last of the mudras, and the widest view of the hand.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `WHERE THE HAND GOES, THE EYES FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: A potter's wheel turns in a narrow lane. Two wet hands close around a lump of clay, and it rises into a wall, then a lip, then a bowl. Next door, a woman's hands press dough flat and slap it onto a hot pan. Across the lane, a shopkeeper counts out change. Nobody here is holding a sacred shape. All week the mudras have been hands that mean something on purpose. Today the Gita puts hands everywhere.
screen: `A POTTER'S HANDS. A COOK'S. A SHOPKEEPER'S.` → `NO SACRED SHAPE.` → `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the thirteenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna describes what is to be known, the one reality behind everything, and the description begins with hands. In paraphrase: its hands and feet are everywhere; its eyes, heads and faces are everywhere; its ears are everywhere; it stands in the world, enfolding all. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad carries the same line, almost word for word. Then the next verse turns it around, in paraphrase: it shines through the workings of all the senses, and yet it is without senses; unattached, and yet it holds everything up. Hands everywhere, and no hands at all. Some commentators say it is spoken of as having hands because of the hands of all beings, through which it works, while it is never bound to any one of them. Some devotees hear something closer to home: the divine at work in every pair of hands. The verse leaves room for both. Now look back at the week of hands. A seal, pressed in so it holds. Anjali, the joined palms, a bow to you. Chin mudra, the small self bending to the great, under a banyan tree. The breathing hand at the nose. Abhaya and varada: do not fear, and give. The dancer's hand, with the eyes and mind following. Each was a hand shaped to carry a meaning. The Gita's line doesn't cancel any of that. It widens it: the hand before a shrine and the hand at the wheel or the stove, named in one breath. Some readers take the verse to say that every hand at work is already held inside a larger one.
screen: `GITA 13: HANDS AND FEET EVERYWHERE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE: AND WITHOUT SENSES.` · `THE WEEK OF SHAPED HANDS.` · `THE SHRINE AND THE STOVE, IN ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `HANDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Rest the hands on the thighs, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, the places that do the work. Close the eyes and let other hands from your day come and go, the ones that grew and cooked your food, the ones that built your chair. Then settle back into your own open palms; if you pray, let the verse rest there, and if not, stay with their warmth and the breath.
The mudras. Today, the widest: what is to be known has hands and feet everywhere, and yet no senses.
Your line: hands and feet everywhere. Tomorrow the hands rest, and the mouth begins. That's day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1040.hook: in the Gita Krishna says that among letters he is the first one, a, the sound of an open mouth
1040.carry: listen for the a inside it
1040.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1040.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn the alphabet aloud, in its traditional order from vowels to consonants grouped by where the mouth makes them, often reciting it with a teacher before reading texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the mudras with the Gita's widest picture: hands and feet everywhere, and yet no senses at all. Today the mouth takes over from the hands.

Open a careful English edition of the Gita and the names start growing small marks. A line over a letter. A dot underneath. An accent perched on an s. It's easy to skip them and say the word the way it looks in English. But every mark is a direction for the mouth: how a page of English letters carries a language built to be heard. This week, one alphabet, learned the way it was meant to be learned: by sound.
screen: `A LINE OVER, A DOT UNDER.` → `EVERY MARK IS A DIRECTION.` → `AN ALPHABET LEARNED BY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse. In the tenth chapter of the Gita, Krishna names, kind by kind, where he can be found. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among trees, the sacred fig. And at verse thirty-three, in paraphrase: among letters, I am the letter a. Not a grand letter. The plainest one, the sound you make when you open your mouth and let the voice out without shaping it at all. A. That letter is where the Sanskrit alphabet begins, and the whole order is a journey from there. The vowels come first. Then the consonants, arranged by where in the mouth they're made, moving forward from the throat toward the lips. Say the alphabet in order and the sound walks out of you. There's a second gift in that small letter. In Devanagari, the script Sanskrit is often written in today, a consonant on its own already carries a short a. The letter for k is read ka; the letter for m is read ma. Unless a mark says otherwise, the a is there, quietly, in almost every letter on the page. So Krishna's line has a reader's meaning too: the plainest sound runs through all the others. At least one Upanishad treats pronunciation as something taught with care. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens a lesson by announcing shiksha, the teaching of sound, and lists what it covers: the letter, the pitch, the length, the effort, the evenness, the joining. That's this week. Not grammar, not vocabulary. Just the sounds, so the names you already read can be said the way they were heard.
screen: `GITA 10.33: AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.` · `FROM THE THROAT TOWARD THE LIPS.` · `A HIDES INSIDE EVERY CONSONANT.` · `SHIKSHA: THE TEACHING OF SOUND.` · then, large: `THE PLAINEST SOUND RUNS THROUGH ALL.`

segments.voice: Let the jaw soften, breathe in through the nose, and on the out-breath let a quiet, unshaped sound come out: a, like the start of the word about. Let it last as long as the breath, then rest in the silence and notice where the sound seemed to come from. One a on each out-breath; if sound isn't possible where you are, say it inwardly.
A. The open mouth, the plainest sound, the letter Krishna names in the Gita, hidden inside almost every letter on the page.
Your line: listen for the a inside it. Rama, Shiva, karma: it's in every one. Day one thousand forty, done.

1041.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1041.hook: a small line over one letter in Rāma tells the voice to stay longer there
1041.carry: let one long vowel be long
1041.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1041.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn short and long vowels as pairs, and reciters of verses keep the lengths carefully, since the rhythm of a verse depends on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plainest letter, a, the one Krishna names in the Gita, hidden in almost every consonant. Today, the same sound, held longer.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `A: THE OPEN MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Write the name of the prince of Ayodhya in careful English letters and it looks like this: R, a with a small line over it, m, a. Rāma. The line sits on the first a only. The second a has nothing. It's a tiny mark, easy to treat as decoration, easy for the eye to slide past. But it's an instruction about time. It tells the voice where to stay and where to move on.
screen: `RĀMA: A LINE OVER ONE A.` → `NOT DECORATION.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT TIME.`

segments.voice: The Upanishad's list for the teaching of sound included matra: length, the measure of a sound in time. Sanskrit vowels come in short and long pairs. Short a, long ā. Short i, long ī. Short u, long ū. In Devanagari the long vowel has its own letter or sign; in English transliteration, it gets a small line on top. That line means: hold this one longer. The tradition of reciting measures it in units it calls matras: a short vowel takes one, a long vowel about two. Now listen to names you know. Rāma: the first syllable long, the second short. Rah-muh. Sītā: both long. See-tah. Gītā, as in the Bhagavad Gita: also both long, so the name ends on an open ah, not a clipped uh. And words where nothing is long. Karma: kur-muh. Shiva: shi-vuh. Nothing is wrong with how English speakers say these names; anyone who hears them will know who you mean. But length changes the music. Much Sanskrit verse is measured in light and heavy syllables, and vowel length helps decide which is which, so length is part of a line's rhythm, the way beats are part of a song. Stretch the wrong syllable and a chanted verse starts to limp. Get the lengths right and it walks the way it was made to walk. That's why the little line matters. It isn't about sounding impressive. It's a way of hearing the text as its reciters heard it, one measured breath of sound after another.
screen: `MATRA: LENGTH, A SOUND'S MEASURE IN TIME.` · `SHORT A, LONG Ā. SHORT I, LONG Ī.` · `RĀMA, SĪTĀ, GĪTĀ. KARMA, SHIVA.` · `LENGTH IS PART OF THE RHYTHM.` · then, large: `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say a short a, quick and soft, then a long ā, held about twice as long: one is a step, the other a stride. Then say a name slowly, Rāma, long then short, or Sītā, long then long, letting the line over the letter decide how long you stay. If you pray, let a name you pray with carry this rhythm; if not, just listen to the measure.
Matra. The length of a sound in time: short and long vowels, and the small line over a letter that means stay longer.

1042.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1042.hook: ka, cha, ta, ta, pa: say the consonant rows in order and the sound walks from the throat to the lips
1042.carry: find where in the mouth it lives
1042.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1042.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit recite the consonants row by row, ka-kha-ga-gha-nga and onward, learning each row by where the mouth makes it, from the throat to the lips.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matra: the line over a letter means a long vowel, stay longer. Rāma, long then short. Today the consonants, and a map of the mouth.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: A chakra, in a scholar's book, is spelled c, a, k, r, a. Cakra. A reader who has heard the word chakra all their life stops and frowns. Did someone drop a letter? No. In the careful system of spelling Sanskrit in English letters, c is always said ch, as in church. It looks like a typo until you know the map behind it: the consonants laid out in rows, each row a place in your own mouth.
screen: `CAKRA, NOT A TYPO.` → `C IS ALWAYS CH.` → `A MAP OF THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the map. Say each sound slowly and feel where it lands. The first row is made at the back, in the throat: ka, kha, ga, gha, and a nasal, nga. The second row moves forward to the palate, where the middle of the tongue rises: cha, chha, ja, jha, and nya. The third row is made with the tip of the tongue curled up to the roof of the mouth; that row gets its own day tomorrow. The fourth row comes forward again, the tongue touching the teeth: ta, tha, da, dha, na. And the last row is made at the lips: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips. Say the first sound of each row in order, ka, cha, ta, ta, pa, and the sound walks forward out of you. Every row ends the same way, with a sound that hums through the nose. And inside each row, plain sounds sit beside breathy ones, ka beside kha; that pattern gets its own day soon. The Upanishad's list for the teaching of sound starts with the letter, varna, and laid out this way the alphabet is more than a list to memorize. It's a description of the body speaking. For a reader, the map does real work. It explains why c is ch: it lives in the palate row. Cakra is chakra. Candra, the moon, is chandra. And when you meet a strange spelling, you can ask one useful question: where in the mouth does this sound live? Find the place, and the sound usually follows.

segments.voice: One out-breath at a time, say slowly: ka, at the back of the throat; cha, the middle of the tongue rising; ta, the tongue curled back; ta, at the teeth; pa, at the lips. Rest a breath, then walk the sounds forward again, slowly enough to feel each place. End with the hum that closes the last row, ma, and let it fade into the breath.

1043.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1043.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit practice the retroflex row (ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa) by curling the tongue back to the roof of the mouth, and recite names like Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu with these sounds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ka and the map of the mouth: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips, and c always said ch. The roof was skipped. Today it gets its turn, and the week gets a look back.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.`

segments.voice: Krishna, the way a scholar spells it, has dots hanging under its letters. K. R with a dot. S with a dot. N with a dot. A. Kṛṣṇa. It can look fussy, like footnotes that wandered into the middle of a word. But the dots point to the place skipped yesterday, the roof of the mouth. They tell the tongue to do one thing: curl back.
screen: `KṚṢṆA: A DOT UNDER R, S AND N.` → `NOT FOOTNOTES.` → `THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.`

segments.voice: Put the tip of your tongue behind your top teeth and say ta. That's the teeth row. Now slide the tip back along the roof of your mouth, past the ridge, and curl it up a little. Say ta from there. The sound gets deeper, almost hollow. That's the roof row, and in transliteration its letters get a dot underneath: ṭa, ḍa, ṇa. Linguists call these sounds retroflex: made with the tongue bent back. The same curl gives a second kind of sh. Plain sh, written with an accent on the s, sits at the palate: Śiva. The s with a dot under it is sh with the tongue curled back: Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa. And the r with a dot under it is something else again: a vowel. Sanskrit treats a lightly rolled r as a vowel sound in its own right, ṛ. How it's said depends on where you learned it. Some reciters say it close to ri, which is where the English spelling Krishna comes from. Others, in parts of the south and west, say it closer to ru. Both are living ways of saying the same letter. So the name can be read in full: kṛ, with the r-vowel; ṣ, the curled sh; ṇa, the curled n. Now look back at the week. The mudras ended with hands that were received, danced, and found everywhere. Then the sounds began: a, the plainest letter; the line that says stay longer; the map of the mouth; and today, the dot that curls the tongue. Hands, then mouth. Each one a way of letting the body carry meaning.
screen: `THE ROOF ROW: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · `Ś AT THE PALATE, Ṣ CURLED BACK.` · `Ṛ: THE R THAT IS A VOWEL.` · `THE WEEK: HANDS, THEN MOUTH.` · then, large: `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Say ta at the teeth, then curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof, back and forth a few times; then na and ṇa the same way. Then say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa. However you've always said it is fine; this is just listening to what the dots ask for, and if you pray, you can let the name be said with care.
